speakers.name: Dame Diana Johnson
speakers.role: The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety

contributions.text: I call Samantha Niblett, who will speak for up to 15 minutes.
contributions.name: Chair

contributions.text: I beg to move, That this House has considered lifelong sex education. Back in March, I successfully applied for this debate on lifelong sex education. In April, alongside Cindy Gallop of MakeLoveNotPorn, I launched “Yes, Sex Please! We’re British!”, a campaign for lifelong sex education. At its heart are two ambitions: first, to create happier, healthier and better-connected humans by taking away the shame, guilt and embarrassment that too often surround conversations about sex, bodies, relationships and intimacy; and secondly, to make it harder for perpetrators of sexual abuse to thrive in precisely that silence, shame and embarrassment. I am so proud of this Labour Government’s violence against women and girls strategy, which my campaign seeks to support, but we must also acknowledge that girls and women are not the only victims of sexual abuse. Boys and men are victims and survivors too, and trans people face particularly high risks. When it comes to shame, there is only one place it should live. As the extraordinary Gisèle Pelicot said, shame needs to change sides—from the survivor to the perpetrator. Recently, we have witnessed enormous courage from women speaking publicly abo
contributions.name: Samantha Niblett

contributions.text: I congratulate my hon. Friend on launching this campaign. I am sure that she has been called brave many times for talking about these issues, but I am not sure that anyone should have to be brave to do so. I admire the way that she talks about sex education and sex lives in the way that normal people do. Does she agree that lifelong sex education should reflect the diversity of normal people’s experiences, and that it should be relevant and useful throughout to people who are gay, lesbian, trans and others? On that basis, will she join me in thanking institutions and organisations such as the Eddystone Trust, Intercom Trust and others for the work they do to reach diverse audiences?
contributions.name: Steve Race

contributions.text: I thank my hon. Friend for his intervention—he has put words in my mouth, frankly. Just this week I had a call with the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV, where we talked in particular about the kind of sex education that is available for trans people, which, quite frankly, is non-existent. There is a lot of work for us to do there, because we cannot be what we cannot see. To empower everybody, we all need to have access to good, relevant and accurate information. So we are risking people not reaching the services they need, and they may not even be available. Yet the reported 86% reduction in the most dangerous HPV infections shows something equally important: good information, prevention and accessible healthcare work. Yesterday, I asked the Natsal panel what one thing they wanted me to bring to this debate, and their message was that we must bring sexual wellbeing into everything. Sexual wellbeing means feeling respected, safe, at ease and supported, with self-worth and agency in relation to sex and sexuality. That leads me to my first ask of Ministers. contributions.name: Samantha Niblett

contributions.text: In my previous life I worked for a social housing association and we provided accommodation for people with learning disabilities. We were engaged with the Supported Loving initiative, and one thing that was transformative was seeing how having good, positive conversations with people with learning disabilities enhanced their wellbeing overall.
contributions.name: Amanda Hack

contributions.text: I thank my hon. Friend for her intervention. That is something that constituents have commented on too. Just yesterday, when I posted about Natsal, somebody commented, “Please make sure you are including people with special needs and disabilities in this campaign”. I was very proud to reply that it is already in my speech. People with learning disabilities and autistic people have the same right as everybody else to positive, loving, safe and fulfilling relationships, and to desire and to be desired. The same principle must also extend to deaf people. Teacher of the deaf Claire Cummings has highlighted how communication barriers can exclude deaf children from the informal learning about relationships, consent and boundaries that hearing children may absorb through everyday conversations. Education should therefore be accessible, including through British Sign Language, and designed with deaf people themselves. Lifelong sex health education should not ignore miscarriage either. Miscarriage UK has rightly argued for accurate, compassionate information about miscarriage, support and its physical and emotional effects. contributions.name: Samantha Niblett

contributions.text: I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) on securing this debate and on her fantastic work on the brilliant “Yes, sex please! We’re British!” campaign; I thank her for it too. She has been rightly bold in knocking down some of the barriers that have historically surrounded conversations about sex, sexual health and relationships. Her work on the issue has been groundbreaking and stigma-breaking, and that should be warmly welcomed in all quarters. I have to say that I have been deeply disappointed to see some of the coverage of my hon. Friend’s work in the media, particularly the reductive nature of some responses, reducing what is an important and serious campaign to nicknames like “the sex MP” or a juvenile obsession with the suggestion that sex toys might be brought into Portcullis House, as if they are something shameful or inappropriate that should not be brought into a place like this, where we can and should debate all aspects of our health and wellbeing. contributions.name: Josh Newbury

contributions.text: I congratulate the hon. Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) on securing this important debate. She talks passionately about sexual health and wellbeing. I commend her for addressing some important topics that are not spoken about enough in a sensible and reasonable way, and for calling for a public health campaign. It is a huge shame that this campaign was sidelined by the conversation about bringing sex toys into Parliament. That overshadowed what should and could be an important conversation. Lifelong sex education covers a huge amount of ground, from physical health to building the confidence and boundaries that people need throughout their lives. The Liberal Democrats welcome that wider conversation. Yet none of it works unless we get the fundamentals right, and that means teaching everyone to understand and respect consent because when we fail to do that, it is mostly women and girls who pay the price. contributions.name: Caroline Voaden

contributions.who: The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety (Dame Diana Johnson)
contributions.text: I start by congratulating my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) on securing this debate on a subject that is fundamental to people’s health and wellbeing, and one that sometimes is not discussed openly. Healthy relationships, sexual wellbeing and the ability to make informed choice is important throughout adulthood. I note that my hon. Friend is the chair of the all-party group on sexual and reproductive health in the UK. I thank her for her work in that role, which I held for several years. Cross-party working ensured that we saw progress on abortion provision, the decriminalisation of abortion for women, and easier access to the morning-after pill and other contraception through pharmacies. I am slightly taken aback to be called so early in the debate, and to see that the Opposition have not responded to the debate. I was very much looking forward to hearing from the hon. Member for Bridlington and The Wolds (Charlie Dewhirst), my near neighbour in East Yorkshire, who might have said some very interesting things. I know that many Opposition Members have—
contributions.name: Dame Diana Johnson
contributions.role: The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety

contributions.text: Well, I have been in the House for 21 years, and the expectation is that His Majesty’s loyal Opposition will field someone on the Front Bench to give the Opposition’s view in debates. As I said, I am slightly surprised that we will not have the benefit of hearing from an Opposition Front Bencher, because I know that many Opposition Members have good, strong views about what healthy relationships look like, and are concerned about issues such as consent, violence against women and girls and the misogyny in our society. That is disappointing, but I will move on to the excellent speech from my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury). As ever, he made a very considered contribution to the debate, with some very interesting points about consent and pornography in particular. Before I address relationships, sex and health education, I want to make this point: families are one of the first ways that a young person can be shown what a good, healthy, loving relationship can look like. contributions.name: Dame Diana Johnson
contributions.role: The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety

contributions.text: I call Samantha Niblett to wind up.
contributions.name: Chair

contributions.text: I thank the Minister for such a wonderful and considered response. I can genuinely say that I feel really heard, and it sounds to me like we have the beginning of a national strategy. I thank my hon. Friends the Members for Exeter (Steve Race) and for North West Leicestershire (Amanda Hack), who are no longer in their places, for their interventions about the importance of inclusivity in sex education and ensuring that we are including the LGBT community, as well as people who have learning disabilities. My hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) is one of my favourite MPs, and he always speaks so beautifully and eloquently. Many hon. Members have praised me for the work that I am doing, but they have not felt bold or brave enough to come and speak in the debate. We say we need male role models, and I cannot think of anyone greater to be a male role model than my hon. Friend. [Hon. Members: “Ahh!”] It feels as if those are quite condescending “ahhs” coming from the Conservative Benches—I hope they are well meant.
